also called the '''FTSE 100 Index''', '''FTSE 100''', '''FTSE''' or, informally, the "'''Footsie'''" {{IPAc-en|ˈ|f|ʊ|t|s|i}}, is the United Kingdom's best-known [[stock market index]] and represents the 100 most [[market capitalisation|highly capitalised]] [[blue chip (stock market)|blue chips]] listed on the [[London Stock Exchange]].{{cite web |url = https://www.lseg.com/en/ftse-russell/indices/uk |title=FTSE UK Index Series |publisher = FTSE Russell |website = LSEG |access-date = 27 February 2024}} ==History== The index started on 3 January 1984,{{cite web|url=https://research.ftserussell.com/Analytics/Factsheets/Home/DownloadSingleIssue?issueName=UKX&IsManual=false|title=FTSE 100 Index Factsheet|access-date=3 February 2023|publisher=FTSE Russell|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240214213600/https://research.ftserussell.com/Analytics/Factsheets/Home/DownloadSingleIssue?issueName=UKX&IsManual=false|archive-date=14 February 2024}}{{cite web |url = https://www.londonstockexchange.com/indices/ftse-100 |title=FTSE overview |website = London Stock Exchange |access-date = 27 February 2024}} having been constructed by the [[London Stock Exchange]] to better reflect activity on the market. The index would replace the ''[[Financial Times]]''{{'}} own [[FT 30]] after its public unveiling on 14 February.{{Harvnb|Michie|1999|pp=573}}{{cite web|url=https://stockmarketalmanac.co.uk/2014/01/ftse-100-index-30-years-old-today/|title=FTSE 100 Index – 30 years old today|date=3 January 2014|publisher=Stock Market Almanack|access-date=30 December 2020|archive-date=23 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200923131032/http://stockmarketalmanac.co.uk/2014/01/ftse-100-index-30-years-old-today/|url-status=dead}}{{Harvnb|Makepeace|2020|pp=51}} As late as 10 February, the Stock Exchange referred to the index as 'SE 100', cutting out the ''Financial Times'' who had not contributed to its construction. Recognition was ultimately given to the fact that having the FT involved in the official launch possessed value.{{Harvnb|Kynaston|1997|pp=133}} The new index allowed the Stock Exchange's own London Traded Options Market (LTOM) to launch an [[option (finance)|options contract]] derived from the FTSE's real-time data in May 1984, while competitors [[London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange|LIFFE]] were quick to coincide their launch of the [[futures contract]].{{cite web |last1=Scott |first1=Gordon |title=LIFFE |url=https://www.investopedia.com/terms/l/liffe.asp |website=investopedia |accessdate=2020-08-12}}{{Harvnb|Kynaston|1997|pp=131}}{{Harvnb|Michie|1999|pp=573}} Usage of the index grew, although the tradeable index contracts struggled to gain traction: annual volume on the FTSE futures contract fell short of 89,000 in 1985, pale in comparison to the 15 million lots traded on the [[S&P 500]] index contract.{{Harvnb|Kynaston|1997|pp=328}} By 1986, [[Margaret Thatcher]]'s sweeping financial deregulation and high profile privatisations of index members [[BT Group|British Telecom]], [[British Gas]], and [[British Aerospace]] had culminated in the [[Big Bang (financial markets)|Big Bang]].{{cite web |title=FTSE 100 index turns forty |url=https://www.lseg.com/content/dam/ftse-russell/en_us/documents/research/ftse-100-index-turns-forty.pdf |website=FTSE Russell |accessdate=2024-06-02}} The combination of a new index, major privatisations, LIFFE tradable derivatives, and promotion by the Financial Times led to the FTSE 100 becoming the most widely used indicator of whether the UK stock market was rising or falling.{{Harvnb|Michie|1999|pp=574}} In 1987, privatisations continued with [[British Airways]] and [[British Petroleum]]. The latter concluded on the same day as [[Black Monday (1987)|Black Monday]], a crash in which the index fell 21.73% in two days; one of those days is still the index's worst single-day return, –12.22%. While the index was in freefall, trading volume of the futures contract hit a record high of 9,111 contracts in a single day. By comparison, the volume in the week preceding the crash averaged 2,400 contracts per day.{{Harvnb|Kynaston|1997|pp=178}} By the spring of 1992, LTOM was sold to LIFFE for a nominal sum, consolidating derivatives of the FTSE 100 index into one exchange.{{Harvnb|Kynaston|1997|pp=256}}{{Harvnb|Michie|1999|pp=618}}{{cite web|url=https://www.fia.org/marketvoice/articles/liffe-story-remembering-sir-brian-williamson-and-his-invaluable-contribution|title=Liffe story: Remembering Sir Brian Williamson and his invaluable contribution to futures|publisher=FIA Market Voice|date=14 November 2024|access-date=5 May 2025}} Trading of these instruments remained solely in the [[Institutional investor|institutional]] domain since the significant investment required to deliver [[electronic trading]] limited retail access at the time.{{Harvnb|Kynaston|1997|pp=207}} Nonetheless annual volumes for 1992 in FTSE futures and options contracts hit a new high of 2.6 million and 2.2 million respectively.{{Harvnb|Kynaston|1997|pp=329}} In the autumn the [[Bank of England]] directed by [[HM Treasury]] under [[John Major]]'s government failed to prop up [[Pound sterling|sterling]] to maintain the [[European Exchange Rate Mechanism]]. A swift [[devaluation]] of sterling on [[Black Wednesday]] and exit from the [[European Exchange Rate Mechanism|ERM]] benefitted the globally trading FTSE index constituents enormously as [[exports]] became cheaper overnight.{{Harvnb|Kynaston|1997|pp=257}} Closing on 15 September 1992 at 2,370.0, the index would almost triple by the end of the decade, hitting a high of 6,930.2 on 30 December 1999.{{Cite web |title=Europe caps year with records - Dec. 30, 1999 |url=https://money.cnn.com/1999/12/30/europe/markets_europe/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210623084955/https://money.cnn.com/1999/12/30/europe/markets_europe/ |archive-date=2021-06-23 |access-date=2026-02-13 |website=money.cnn.com}} In 2024, there were the most delistings from the London market since the [[2008 financial crisis]], with companies citing higher valuations and lower costs available by switching to [[New York Stock Exchange|NYSE]]. Among them [[Ashtead Group]], [[CRH plc|CRH]], and [[Flutter Entertainment|Flutter]] represented almost £120 billion in FTSE 100 [[market capitalisation]]. Takeovers from [[private equity]] further reduced the available pool of companies that could be drawn on to populate the index, with [[Hargreaves Lansdown]] also set to delist. Across the entire exchange there were five delistings for every new issue, with speculation at the close of the year around the future of index stalwarts [[British American Tobacco]], [[Rio Tinto (corporation)|Rio Tinto]], and [[Shell plc|Shell]].{{cite web |date=15 December 2024 |title=London Stock Exchange suffers biggest exodus since financial crisis |url=https://www.ft.com/content/aef053ce-c94d-4a72-8dce-bdbf56dd67e1 |accessdate=2025-01-24 |website=Financial Times}} ==Description== The [[stock market index|index]] has trading symbol UKX and is maintained by [[FTSE Russell]], a wholly owned [[subsidiary]] of [[London Stock Exchange Group]], which originated as a joint venture between the ''[[Financial Times]]'' and the London Stock Exchange. It is calculated in [[Real-time computing|real time]] and published every second when the market is open. The FTSE 100 broadly consists of the largest 100 qualifying UK companies by full market value.{{cite web |url=https://www.lseg.com/content/dam/ftse-russell/en_us/documents/ground-rules/ftse-uk-index-series-ground-rules.pdf |title=FTSE UK Index Series Ground Rules, v17.3 |publisher=FTSE Russell |date=September 2026 |format=PDF |access-date=24 October 2026}} The total market value of a company is calculated by multiplying the share price of the company by the total number of shares they have issued. The index therefore only reacts to a change in the market value of the companies, excluding any dividend income an investor may otherwise reinvest. In order to view the effect of both market value performance and income relative to the FTSE 100 Index alone, the FTSE 100 Total Return Index is used. Over the last four decades, the total return index has doubled almost five times whilst the index has doubled slightly more than three times respectively.{{Cite web |title= FTSE 100 TR |url = https://www.lseg.com/en/ftse-russell/indices/uk#overview |website=LSEG |access-date = 18 April 2026 }}[[File:FTSE 100 TR Index Line Chart.png|thumb|Total return index from 1986 thru 2026]] Further, many of these are internationally focused companies: therefore the index's movements are a fairly weak indicator of how the UK economy is faring and are significantly affected by the [[exchange rate]]s of the pound sterling.{{Cite news |last1 = Atkins |first1 = Ralph |last2 = Elder |first2 = Bryce |date = 3 September 2014 |title = FTSE 100 hits new record high on sterling weakness |url = http://www.businessinsider.com/r-ftse-100-hits-new-record-high-on-sterling-weakness-2017-1?IR=T |work = businessinsider.co.uk |access-date = 29 March 2017 }} A better indication of the UK economy is the [[FTSE 250 Index]], as it contains a smaller proportion of international companies.{{cite web|url=http://www.hl.co.uk/shares/share-tips/richard-hunter-weekly-comment/which-indices-best-represent-the-economy |title=Which indices best represent the economy? |work=Hargreaves Lansdown |access-date=9 May 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130602082259/http://www.hl.co.uk/shares/share-tips/richard-hunter-weekly-comment/which-indices-best-represent-the-economy |archive-date=2 June 2013 }} Even though the [[FTSE All-Share Index]] is more comprehensive, the FTSE 100 is by far the most widely used UK stock market indicator. Other related indices are the FTSE 250 Index (which includes the next largest 250 companies after the FTSE 100), the [[FTSE 350 Index]] (which is the aggregation of the FTSE 100 and 250), [[FTSE SmallCap Index]] and the [[FTSE Fledgling Index]]. The FTSE All-Share aggregates the FTSE 100, FTSE 250 and FTSE SmallCap. The index consists of 18 [[Industry Classification Benchmark|ICB]] [[business sector|Supersectors]], four of which had a market capitalisation exceeding £250 billion {{As of|2026|September|30|lc=y}}. These are [[banking in the United Kingdom|Banks]], [[Pharmaceutical industry in the United Kingdom|Health Care]], [[Oil and gas industry in the United Kingdom|Energy]] and [[Aerospace industry in the United Kingdom|Industrial Goods and Services]], which together account for approximately 55% of the index's capitalisation. On the same date, there were two companies with a market cap exceeding £200 billion: [[HSBC]] and [[Shell plc|Shell]], which together accounted for approximately 18% of the market cap.{{cite web |url = https://research.ftserussell.com/Analytics/FactSheets/Home/DownloadSingleIssue?issueName=UKX&isManual=False |title=FTSE 100 Factsheet (data as at 30 September 2026) |website = LSEG |access-date = 24 October 2026}} {{Bar chart | title = ICB Supersector Marketcap to the nearest billion £ sterling as at September 2026 | label_type = ICB Supersector | data_type = Marketcap (£ billion) | bar_width = 20 | width_units = em | data_max = 485 | label1 = Banks | data1 = 485 | label2 = Health Care | data2 = 300 | label3 = Energy | data3 = 295 | label4 = Industrial Goods and Services | data4 = 294 | label5 = Basic Resources | data5 = 201 | label6 = Personal Care Drug and Grocery Stores | data6 = 170 | label7 = Food Beverage and Tobacco | data7 = 167 | label8 = Financial Services | data8 = 134 | label9 = Utilities | data9 = 118 | label10 = Insurance | data10 = 89 | label11 = Technology | data11 = 59 | label12 = Consumer Products and Services | data12 = 52 | label13 = Travel and Leisure | data13 = 40 | label14 = Telecommunications | data14 = 35 | label15 = Real Estate | data15 = 29 | label16 = Retailers | data16 = 28 | label17 = Media | data17 = 18 | label18 = Chemicals | data18 = 5 }} Each calendar quarter, the FTSE's constituents are reviewed and some companies exit or enter the index, resulting in irregular [[Volume (finance)|trading volume]] and price changes as [[market participant]]s rebalance their [[Portfolio (finance)|portfolios]]. ===Weighting=== In the FTSE indices, share prices are weighted by free-float capitalisation, so that the larger companies, with more of their stock "floating", make more of a difference to the index than smaller companies. The basic formula for these indices is:{{cite web|url=https://www.lseg.com/content/dam/ftse-russell/en_us/documents/ground-rules/ftse-uk-index-series-guide-to-calculation.pdf|title=Guide to calculation|publisher=London Stock Exchange|access-date=11 May 2025|archive-date=6 March 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240306050020/https://www.lseg.com/content/dam/ftse-russell/en_us/documents/ground-rules/ftse-uk-index-series-guide-to-calculation.pdf|url-status=dead}} \begin{align} \mathrm{Index~value} &= \frac{\mathrm{Total~market~value}}{\mathrm{Index~divisor}} \end{align} expanded to, \begin{align} \mathrm{Index~value} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left ( \mathrm{Price~of~stock}_{i,t}\times\mathrm{Number~of~shares}_{i,t} \times\mathrm{Free~float~factor}_{i,t} \right )}{\mathrm{Index~divisor}} \end{align} where the sum of the products of the price, shares, and FFF for each component beginning at i=1 through to, usually, n=100 at time t are divided by the index~divisor to give the index~value. The free float factor represents the percentage of all issued shares that are readily available for trading; FTSE Russell applies each company's actual free float, and a company must have a free float of at least 10% to be eligible for the index. The free-float capitalisation of a company is its [[market capitalisation]] multiplied by its free float adjustment factor. It therefore does not include restricted stocks, such as those held by company insiders. It follows that the index~divisor at any chosen time, when there are no changes, is derived by rearranging the basic formula to give: \begin{align} \mathrm{Index~divisor} &= \frac{\mathrm{Total~market~value}}{\mathrm{Index~value}} \end{align} However, as with any price index the FTSE 100 Index is always changing, whether by corporate action or constituent change. In order to maintain a true reflection of market price movements the index~divisor is adjusted to mitigate any effect these changes have on the index value. [[FTSE Russell]] employs the index formula developed by [[Hermann Paasche]] for adjusting the index~divisor for values preceding a corporate action and uses the change in the index~value arising from the adjusted divisor to calculate the new value on the day of the corporate action. The Paasche formula is given as: \begin{align} \mathrm{I}_{t}^{Paas} &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{P}_{i,t}\mathrm{Q}_{i,t}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{P}_{i,0}\mathrm{Q}_{i,t}} \end{align} where,
{| |- | \mathrm{I}_{t}^{Paas} | = Paasche Index |- | \mathrm{P}_{i,t} | = price at start of day t for constituent i after adjustments for action or event |- | \mathrm{P}_{i,0} | = price of constituent i on the starting day of calculating the index |- | \mathrm{Q}_{i,t} | = number of shares included in the index for constituent i at the start of day t |}
Since the index is always based on the prior value and not the fixed base value, a Chained Paasche Index is used to chain each new value with the last continuously. This is given by the formula: \begin{align} \mathrm{I}_{t}^{Paas} &= \mathrm{I}_{t-1}^{Paas} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{P}_{i,t}\mathrm{Q}_{i,t}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{P}_{i,t-1}\mathrm{Q}_{i,t}} \end{align} In isolation, the Chained Paasche Index will not adjust the prior closing value, resulting in an abnormal price difference. FTSE Russell utilises a price~adjustment~factor to give continuity, given by the formula: \begin{align} \mathrm{I}_{t}^{Paas} &= \mathrm{I}_{t-1}^{Paas} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{P}_{i,t}\mathrm{Q}_{i,t}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{P}_{i,t-1}\mathrm{Q}_{i,t}\mathrm{PAF}_{i,t}} \end{align} So the index~value or \mathrm{I}_{t}^{Paas} is equal to the product of the previous index~value or \mathrm{I}_{t-1}^{Paas} at time t-1, one period before, and the sum of the products of constituents i through n's price P and quantity Q at time t divided by the sum of the products of constituents i through n's price P at time t-1 and their quantity Q and their price~adjustment~factor at time t. === Futures contracts === The benchmark FTSE 100 futures contracts are traded on the ICE Futures Europe (ICEU) exchange, formerly the London International Financial Futures Exchange ([[London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange|LIFFE]]). The value of each contract is 10 GBP × index points and is specified as:{{Cite web |title=FTSE 100 Index Future |url=https://www.ice.com/products/38716764/FTSE-100-Index-Future |access-date=4 July 2025 |website=ICE Futures Europe |language=en-US}} {| class="wikitable" |+FTSE 100 (Z) contract specifications |- !Contract size |10 GBP × index points |- !Exchange |ICEU |- !Sector |Index |- !Contract Symbol |Z |- !Tick size |0.5 |- !Tick value |5 GBP |- !Basis Point Value |10 |- !Denomination |GBP |- !Decimal places |1 |} On the last trading day of each quarterly futures contract, the settlement price is determined using an intraday auction of all FTSE 100 stocks on the London Stock Exchange, starting at 10:15. ==Record values== [[File:FTSE 100 Index Line Chart (1984-2024) v1.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|Performance of the FTSE 100 index between January 1984 and June 2026]] The index has reached the following record values: {| class="wikitable" |- | Category | colspan="2"|All-time highs |- | Closing ||10,910.55|| 27 February 2026 |- | Intraday ||10,989.45|| 31 July 2026 |- |} The index began on 3 January 1984 at the base level of 1,000. Retrieved 8 August 2008 It was established in 1935 and nowadays is largely obsolete due to its redundancy. It is similar to the [[Dow Jones Industrial Average]], and companies listed are from the industrial and commercial sectors. Financial sector companies and government stocks are excluded. Of the original constituents,{{cite web|url=http://www.ft.com/cms/78c12166-0773-11db-9067-0000779e2340.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221210/http://www.ft.com/cms/78c12166-0773-11db-9067-0000779e2340.html |archive-date=10 December 2022 |url-access=subscription|title=FT30 - the UK's oldest surviving stock market index - FT.com|work=ft.com|access-date=24 February 2015}} three are currently in the FTSE 100: Tate & Lyle, Imperial Tobacco and Rolls-Royce, although Rolls-Royce has not been continuously listed and Imperial Tobacco was a subsidiary of [[Hanson plc|Hanson]] for a number of years, and is now renamed as Imperial Brands. Only one of the original FT 30 companies is still in that index:[http://www.ft.com/cms/28e9d8dc-0781-11db-9067-0000779e2340.html Remaining companies in the FT30] Tate & Lyle (membership is not strictly based on market capitalisation, so this does not mean they are necessarily among the top thirty companies in the FTSE 100).
